extracted.intended_audience: aspiring literary critics and cultivated readers (early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for composing and judging literary criticism and for comportment in refined action — covering what makes a good critic, tone of critique, emphasis on excellencies, and related social virtues (liberality, decency, humility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of a good critic
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic must have a broad insight into the parts of learning, mastery of language, logic, and the ability to convey thoughts with clearness and perspicuity; those who cannot distinguish between words and things, range their thoughts, and set them in proper lights will be confused and obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page stresses knowledge of arts and sciences, elegance and delicacy of native tongue, and clear presentation — citing Aristotle as both critic and logician and warning that mere cleverness without learning makes for an 'illiterate heavy Writer' posing as a critic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish words from things; order thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic (and writer) must master the art of distinguishing between words and things and of ranging and setting thoughts in proper lights so the author's notions are not lost in confusion and obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure here leads to confused thinking and poor expression; Locke's Essay is noted as odd for a would-be critic because it neglects this art. Emphasizes ordering ideas as a technical skill of good criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on superficial rules and cant
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute a few general rules or a 'certain Cant of Words' (e.g., borrowed French formulas) for genuine learning and sound judgment in criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that a few rules from French authors plus a cant of phrases will sometimes set up an illiterate writer as a dangerous critic; originality of judgment and learning are required rather than formulaic application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize excellencies; seek concealed beauties
rubrics_metrics.description: A true critic ought to dwell rather upon Excellencies than Imperfections, to discover the concealed Beauties of a writer and communicate to the world what is worth their observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should highlight and explain merits that less-informed readers might miss; this helps education of taste and protects delicate beauties from crude ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid petty fault-finding and exclusive focus on small errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware the critic who praises only what the public already applauds and turns wholly upon little faults and errors; such fault-finding is easy and common but not the mark of good criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary readers will often ridicule surface errors, but a cultivated critic should go beyond this; the text quotes Dryden ('Errors, like Straws... He who would search for Pearls must dive below') and gives the Apollo/chaff story as an allegory of critics who collect only faults and are rewarded with chaff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use ridicule or ill-placed wit to attack beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule and misplaced wit are unseasonable in criticism; they prejudice readers rather than convince and can turn a beauty into the subject of derision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A little wit can both expose beauty and aggravate a fault; attacking 'verbum ardens' or glowing bold expression with cold ridicule is facile but unjust. Critics should avoid merriment used merely to exercise a talent for ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a serious and instructive tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of criticism should generally appear with a serious and instructive air, following the greatest masters, ancient and modern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts frivolous, laughing critics with the manner of the greatest critics, recommending sobriety and instruction rather than light mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value genius with lapses over inferior exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: The productions of a great genius, even with many lapses and inadvertencies, are infinitely preferable to the works of inferior authors that are scrupulously exact and conformable to all rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longinus is cited to support the view that originality and greatness outweigh pedantic correctness; criticism should allow for and recognize the superiority of genius despite faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform actions (and virtues) in the best and most becoming manner
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice of every virtue there is an additional grace or decency required; men should not be content to barely do well but perform everything in the best and most becoming manner they are able.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Pliny's letter: a benefaction done with good grace, cheerfulness, and an air of pleasure doubles the kindness and ornament; manner and comeliness add lustre to actions (examples: Titian's sunshine, Caesar gathering his robe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality should be cheerful and exceed expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality (giving, benefaction) should be performed with such cheerfulness as to express God-like pleasure in obliging fellow-creatures and should even out-run the receiver's wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pliny's example (presenting 1250 crowns) shows a gift that both helps and delights; the manner of giving adds to the obligation and softens gifts of art and nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wealth for public good and charitable education
rubrics_metrics.description: Those with riches should exert benevolence and bounty, supporting institutions (e.g., charity schools) that provide instruction and industry to the poor; charity fosters useful servants and public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues practical reasons to fund charity schools (public good, producing honest artificers, disciplining servants, preventing domestic slanders) and commends giving for public and heavenly ends rather than merely pomp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate fortunate success with moral merit; practise humility
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not judge a person's virtue or merit solely by their success or good fortune; fortune can arise from prudence, rashness, or unforeseen events, and claiming all success for oneself is presumptuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites examples (Richelieu, Pompey, Roman usage of 'Felix'), the Queen Elizabeth medal ('Afflavit Deus et dissipantur') and a Persian fable (drop turned pearl) to argue that humility and recognition of Providence or chance are proper; prudence helps but does not fully command fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marital finance principle: shared interests over separate purses
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriages ought to be unions of shared pleasures, inclinations, and interests; separate purses (e.g., insisting on 'pin-money' as a guarded retreat) are unnatural and can signal distrust or prepare an escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spectator criticizes the modern practice of pin-money as late and potentially dishonourable, arguing that reserved allowances may foster separation of interests and are as unnatural as separate beds.
